Feed-Forward Networks03

Artificial Neurons

  •   (X): The information the neuron is receiving
  •   (ω): defines how important a given input is for the neuron
  •   (b or ω0): A small adjustment to the weighted sum of the inputs
    • Think of this as shifting the neurons threshold to make it harder or easier to activate
  • Summation (Σ): The weighted sum of the inputs and bias
    • represents the neurons "total input", also known as the pre-activation

The summation transforms multiple inputs into one number that summarizes the information that the neuron cares about.

  •   (ϕ): A function applied to the pre-activation of the neuron
  •    (ŷ): The final resulting value from the activation function

Feed-Forward Networks · Neurons05

The XOR Problem

A neuron is capable of drawing a single line, but our data requires two lines to separate. We can have two neurons each create one of the two lines and use a   to combine their output!

Stacking neurons like this, so some take the outputs of others as their inputs, gives a multi-layer perceptron (MLP), or a feed-forward neural network (FFN)

import torch
X = torch.tensor([[50., 43.], [38., 0.], [14., 42.]])
W1 = torch.tensor([[10., -10.], [-10., 10.]])
b1 = torch.tensor([-85., -85.])
A1 = torch.sigmoid(X @ W1.T + b1) # b1 is added to every row
print(X.shape, W1.shape, b1.shape)
print(A1.round(decimals=3))
Output
torch.Size([3, 2]) torch.Size([2, 2]) torch.Size([2])
tensor([[0., 0.],
        [1., 0.],
        [0., 1.]])

similar to sklearn for machine learning, PyTorch is the library we will use to implement all of our neural networks.

The @ symbol is how we multiply matrices and .T gives us the transpose of a matrix

Activation Functions

Critically, activation functions introduce   into the model. This is what allows neural networks to learn complex patterns (beyond just linear relationships).

Z_2 = \bp{X \Omega_1\T + b_1} \Omega_2\T + b_2 \phantom{Z_2} = X \bp{\Omega_2 \Omega_1}\T + \bp{b_1 \Omega_2\T + b_2} \phantom{Z_2} = X \Omega\T + b

If we didn't have activation functions, our neural network would be no more powerful than just a single neuron. However, this power comes at the cost of  .

For our simple neural network, we are using the sigmoid function as the activation function, but it's not the only choice.

Other common options are the hyperbolic tangent and the ReLU function

Universal Approximation Theorem

The universal approximation theorem says a neural network with a single hidden layer, given enough hidden neurons, can approximate any continuous function

Multi-class Classification

Our three output scores aren't probabilities. To turn them into probabilities that add up to 1, we use the   function:

\text{softmax}(z)_i = \frac{e^{z_i}}{\sum_{j=1}^{K} e^{z_j}}

Softmax is the usual activation function for the   of a classifier. With only two classes it's the same as the  .

import torch
import torch.nn as nn
import torch.nn.functional as F
class SimpleNetwork(nn.Module):
def __init__(self):
super(SimpleNetwork, self).__init__()
self.fc1 = nn.Linear(2, 32)
self.fc2 = nn.Linear(32, 16)
self.fc3 = nn.Linear(16, 1)
def forward(self, x):
x = F.relu(self.fc1(x))
x = F.relu(self.fc2(x))
x = torch.sigmoid(self.fc3(x))
return x
criterion = nn.BCELoss()
a.) Draw the computation graph for the network. (4 pts.)

b.) Give the loss of the neural network (L) as a single statement of nested functions. (1 pt.)
